comment: Inbound-protection conformance fixture (SPEC.md §22). Five obligations every conforming AgentMesh participant owes the party it delivers to: duplicate rejection (§22.2), a freshness window (§22.3), correct addressing (§22.4), an inbound size cap (§22.5) and sender-text fencing (§22.6). The TypeScript SDK (sdk-typescript/) and the Rust SDK (sdk-rust/) both implement all five as of 2026-07-27, the Rust side in sdk-rust/src/inbound.rs and wired into both inbound paths in client.rs; Go, Python and C# are expected to be written natively from the specification rather than from a shared library — which is precisely why the obligations need pinned bytes and not only prose. Two correct Ed25519 implementations do not diverge on the signature; they diverge on canonicalization, on whether a character is counted in bytes or code units, and on whether an empty line is joined in. THE FIXTURE IS THE AUTHORITY. When a test against it fails, fix the implementation — never the fixture. A frame whose markers differ by one byte between two SDKs means a receiving agent cannot tell a frame from sender-written content, which is the single failure the fencing exists to prevent. Every case is checkable with no broker, no connection and no clock: where a verdict depends on the recipient's clock the case carries its own `now`.

identities.comment: TEST VECTORS — never real identities, and they control nothing: no account, no credential, no mesh registration. `sender_seed` is the same published seed conformance/manifest-signing.json uses, deliberately, so no additional private-key-shaped string enters the mirror payload. Ed25519 is deterministic (RFC 8032), so every signature below is reproducible byte for byte from that seed and the canonical bytes printed beside it. The recipient and third party never sign anything here, so only their public halves exist; the seeds they were minted from were discarded.

encodings.comment: The three places two independent implementations drift, stated before the cases that depend on them.
encodings.envelope_signature: Ed25519 over the canonical JSON of the envelope with `sig` removed: object keys sorted recursively, no insignificant whitespace, `undefined`-valued keys omitted (SPEC.md §5.3). The `canonical` string beside each envelope below is exactly those bytes, UTF-8.
encodings.sender_text_length: UTF-16 code units of the extracted sender text — not bytes, and not Unicode scalar values. `😀` counts 2. An implementation whose native string type is UTF-8 MUST compute the UTF-16 length (Rust: `s.encode_utf16().count()`). This is the reference implementation's measure and interoperability, not elegance, is the reason it is fixed: a cap that means 65,536 bytes in one SDK and 65,536 code points in another refuses in one place and accepts in the other, and the sender sees an inconsistent mesh.
encodings.structured_payload_serialization: A payload with no text-bearing field is measured as compact JSON (RFC 8259 escaping, no insignificant whitespace). Key ORDER is deliberately not specified: reordering an object's keys cannot change the serialized length, so it cannot change a verdict. A value that cannot be serialized at all is measured as the name of its type; it did not arrive as JSON, so it cannot be large.

duplicate_rejection.comment: §22.2. The memory exists because the live subscription and the offline-mailbox drain can both deliver the SAME envelope (drain overlap, JetStream redelivery), and the handler must run once. Keyed on the pair (from, id), never on `id` alone: `id` is the SENDER's choice, so keying on it alone let one sender suppress another's traffic by guessing or observing an id, and conflated two unrelated senders who happened to pick the same one.

cases.comment: the case the memory is for: second delivery refused, handler invoked once
MUST BOTH BE ACCEPTED. An id-only memory refuses the second, and one sender can then mute another by reusing its ids
MUST BOTH BE ACCEPTED — a fixture of refusals alone is passed by an implementation that refuses everything

ORDERING, and it is normative. Deliver `stale_by_two_hours` on the LIVE path (refused for age), then deliver the identical envelope from the MAILBOX, where the 7-day window would forgive that age. It MUST be refused as a duplicate. An implementation that remembers only what it accepted lets the buffered copy sail past the rejection the live path just made.

What duplicate rejection does NOT cover, made checkable. The memory is bounded on purpose — an unbounded set fed from the wire is a remote memory-exhaustion primitive — so it forgets. Deliver 5001 distinct ids from one sender (`vector-0` … `vector-5000`, all accepted); `vector-0` has now been evicted, and re-delivering it is ACCEPTED. Nothing is broken: the envelope is still inside the freshness window, so accepting it is accepting a message the sender could have re-sent anyway. This is the exact reason §22.3 is not optional — dedup catches a repeat, the window catches the replay dedup has forgotten.

then.comment: and the window is what still refuses it

not_covered.comment: Listed so a future implementer does not read the memory as more than it is, and does not 'fix' it by making it unbounded.
items: Eviction: a duplicate that arrives after its entry was evicted is accepted. Bounded by the freshness window, not by the memory.
Process restart: the memory is in-process and forgets everything on restart. Same bound applies.
Envelope authenticity: this is not a signature check. `from` is trustworthy only because the envelope was verified before the memory was consulted (§5.3).

freshness.comment: §22.3. A signature proves who wrote an envelope, never when — so a signed envelope is a bearer token for as long as anyone accepts it. Two windows because a buffered envelope is old by construction and the live bound cannot apply to it.
freshness.rule: drift = now - ts. Refuse if ts is unparseable. Refuse if drift < -max_clock_skew_ahead_ms. Otherwise accept if drift <= (mailbox ? max_mailbox_age_ms : max_clock_skew_behind_ms).

addressing.comment: §22.4. A signature binds an envelope to its author, not to the subject it arrived on. `to` is the author's statement of who the envelope was for, so an envelope naming somebody else, delivered here, is a replay by a third party. Compared byte for byte against this agent's own id.

size_cap.comment: §22.5. A message far larger than a message is not a message. This bounds the SENDER TEXT extracted from the payload, not the envelope: the envelope as a whole is the transport's own bound (SPEC.md §18.9, NATS `max_payload`), which is orders of magnitude above anything a real turn carries and is usually a vendor default rather than a decision. The comparison is strictly greater-than.
size_cap.text_extraction: (1) a bare string payload IS the sender text. (2) Otherwise walk `text`, `message`, `prompt` in that order and stop at the first that is neither absent nor null: a string value IS the sender text; any other value is SERIALIZED AND MEASURED but is not sender text. (3) Otherwise the whole payload is serialized and measured, and there is no sender text. A value that is measured rather than read as text is never framed — a frame is prose and a number is not — but it does not suppress the frame on a string rung BELOW it: framing walks for the first STRING rung independently of where this measurement stopped (§22.6, and fencing.payload_shape_cases[non_string_rung_does_not_suppress_the_frame_below_it]). The `sender_text` and `sender_text_field` fields on every fencing.payload_shape_cases entry pin this measurement walk case by case, and `framed_field` is stated wherever the frame lands somewhere other than `sender_text_field`.

cases.comment: MUST BE ACCEPTED. The comparison is strictly greater-than: a message at the cap is a legal message
refused. One character is the whole difference, so an off-by-one in either SDK is visible here and nowhere else

a payload with no field on the shape ladder is not a way past the cap: it is measured as compact JSON. `blob` is a string, so this also pins that a string in some OTHER field is measured but never framed
MUST BE ACCEPTED — the previous case must not be passed by refusing all structured input
`null` serializes to the four characters `null`. Pinned because it is surprising, and because an implementation that measures 0 here disagrees with the reference on a payload that really does arrive

MUST BE ACCEPTED at 4. Two emoji are 2 code points, 4 UTF-16 code units and 8 UTF-8 bytes. The cap counts UTF-16 code units, so this is the case that catches an implementation measuring bytes (8, refused) or code points (2, accepted with the wrong number)
the same two emoji against a cap of 3: refused, because 4 > 3. A byte-counting implementation also refuses but for the wrong reason; a code-point-counting one accepts

a sealed payload has no plaintext to measure, so its serialized ciphertext is what meets the cap. The effective plaintext ceiling for a sealed message is therefore roughly three quarters of the cap — the bound fires early rather than late, which is the safe direction

MUST BE ACCEPTED. `0` is the documented off switch, so the length is irrelevant — 1000 is simply larger than every other cap in this file. Turning it off leaves the transport bound as the only ceiling, which is a deployment default rather than a decision

fencing.comment: §22.6, and the one where byte-exactness matters most. The markers and the frame text are a protocol between the SDK and the model reading its output: if two SDKs disagree about them by one byte, a receiving agent cannot tell a frame from sender-written content, and the warning label becomes a thing an attacker can print. A frame is a warning label, not a lock — what it buys is that the model is told which half of what it is reading a stranger wrote, and that the stranger cannot forge the half that says so.
fencing.fence_rule: In this order: (1) every line terminator becomes LF — CRLF, a lone CR, and U+0085 NEL, U+2028 LINE SEPARATOR and U+2029 PARAGRAPH SEPARATOR, which step 2 does not reach; (2) the remaining C0 controls and DEL are removed, tab and LF surviving — which is also why VT (U+000B) and FF (U+000C) are deliberately absent from step 1, since step 2 removes them outright and a character that is not in the output cannot break a line in any renderer; (3) any line CONTAINING a run of three or more hyphens or three or more equals signs is prefixed with one space. Order is normative: the first version of this fence did only step 3 and a single carriage return defeated it, and the three Unicode separators were the same hole with a different byte until 2026-07-26.

documented, not endorsed: the filter covers C0 and DEL only, so C1 controls pass through. The sample is U+009B CSI, the C1 that introduces an ANSI escape sequence. Pinned so the two SDKs agree on the same narrow rule rather than one of them widening it silently. The one C1 that does NOT survive is U+0085 NEL, which step 1 maps to LF because it is a line terminator (see unicode_line_separators_become_lf) — NEL was this case's sample until that was fixed on 2026-07-26.

THE attack the lone-CR fix left behind, closed 2026-07-26. U+2028 LINE SEPARATOR, U+2029 PARAGRAPH SEPARATOR and U+0085 NEL (all three below, in that order) are line terminators in ECMAScript and mandatory breaks in UAX #14, and none of them is CR or a C0 control — so they survived steps 1 and 2, the fence saw one long line and indented it once, and a renderer that honours them showed the reader a forged END marker and a forged operator block each at the start of a line. Step 1 now maps all three to LF. Mapped, not deleted: the sender's intended break survives, and step 3 then examines the line that follows it, which is what indents the forged marker. VT (U+000B) and FF (U+000C) complete the line-terminator class and are deliberately NOT in step 1 — step 2 removes them, and a character that is not in the output cannot break a line.

Closed 2026-07-26, and this case is the pin for the ruling. A non-string `text` stops the MEASUREMENT walk (§22.5, so an oversized number cannot slip past the cap by not being prose) and it used to stop the FRAMING with it: the payload was returned unchanged and the `message` string reached the handler as raw sender prose, with no frame and no warning. The frame now goes on the first STRING rung of the ladder, independently of where the measurement stopped — otherwise a sender decides, with one number, whether the recipient's model is told a stranger wrote what it is reading. `sender_text` and `sender_text_field` still describe the measurement; `framed_field` says where the frame went.

double_fencing.comment: Not a case, a prohibition. Wrapping already-framed text produces two nested frames and indents the inner markers, so the model sees a frame it cannot tell from sender-written text — worse than either alone. A host that frames inbound text itself (because it resolved the sender's handle first, which the SDK's dispatch path does not) MUST turn the SDK's default off rather than accept two frames.

refusals.comment: §22.7. A sender that gets nothing cannot tell a refusal from a crash, and a recipient that is protected in silence cannot tell it is being protected. Each protection's refusal channel, pinned. `error_code` values are SPEC.md §12.2 codes; the human-readable `message` beside them is deliberately NOT pinned — it names SDK-specific option spellings and is not part of the contract.

to_sender.comment: sent wherever a reply path exists. Not retryable: the same bytes will be too big next time

to_recipient.comment: raised even on the mailbox path, where there may be nobody to answer

duplicate.comment: silent. The first copy was answered; answering again would make one delivery look like two, and a duplicate is normal transport behaviour rather than misbehaviour

stale.comment: silent. The party that would receive the answer is whoever replayed it, and an error envelope tells a replayer which of its held copies are still inside the window

misaddressed.comment: silent, for the same reason: replying would confirm to a third party that this inbox is live and would put this agent's signature on a reply to a message it was never sent

envelopes.comment: Fully-formed, really-signed request envelopes so the envelope-level cases above can be exercised end to end without a broker: decode (which verifies `sig` against `from`), then apply the checks. `canonical` is the canonical envelope JSON without the domain prefix; each signature covers signed_bytes_prefix + canonical (SPEC.md 5.3).

addressed_to_recipient.comment: the normal case, and the envelope the accept-side addressing and duplicate cases are built on

addressed_to_a_third_party.comment: a replay onto the recipient's inbox: genuinely signed by the sender, genuinely intended for somebody else. Every agent the sender ever messaged holds one of these and could aim it here

no_to_field.comment: an absent `to` is legitimate — service calls omit it — so this MUST BE ACCEPTED. Note what that means: the addressing check refuses a WRONG destination, it does not require a stated one

to_differs_only_by_case.comment: the last character of the recipient's key lowercased. Refused: an agent id is compared byte for byte, never case-folded or normalised. An implementation that case-folds accepts an envelope addressed to a key that does not exist

stale_by_two_hours.comment: used by the ordering case: refused on the live path for age, and MUST still be remembered by the dedup memory

hops_over_the_relay_bound.comment: meta.hops above the §21 relay bound. Included so the addressing fixture is not read as the only meta-level drop

suspected_gaps.comment: Both cases this block listed were reported to the specification owner on 2026-07-26, ruled DEFECTS the same day, and closed in sdk-typescript/src/internal/fence.ts with the affected cases changed in the same commit. Nothing is pinned as suspected today. The block stays because the discipline it records is the fixture's own: a behaviour nobody has ruled on is still pinned rather than omitted, because an unpinned behaviour is one two implementations can silently disagree about, and a disagreement here is worse than the defect. This is the ONLY place in this fixture where changing a case is the right answer, and only on those terms.

closed.ruling: Defect. U+0085, U+2028 and U+2029 survived both the CR normalisation and the C0 filter, and every one of them is a line terminator to a renderer — so a forged END marker could begin a line the fence never examined, which is the lone-CR defect with a different byte. Step 1 now maps all three to LF. The rest of the line-terminator class was checked: VT (U+000B) and FF (U+000C) are C0, step 2 removes them, and a character absent from the output cannot break a line, so they were deliberately not added. The accept-side cases (two_hyphens_untouched, non_ascii_preserved, astral_plane_preserved) were re-run to confirm the fix does not over-escape.

Defect. A non-string rung stopped the measurement walk and the framing with it, so {"text": 0, "message": "..."} reached the handler with raw sender prose. Framing now takes the first STRING rung whatever the measurement found. Only that one rung is framed — see only_the_first_string_rung_is_framed for the limit and the reason. The §22.5 measurement walk is unchanged, so every size_cap case still holds, and a sealed payload is still returned untouched.

not_covered.comment: Boundaries of §22 as a whole, written down so nobody widens them by accident and nobody mistakes them for gaps.
items: These five are RECEIVER obligations. None of them makes a message safe: a frame is a label, a cap is a bound, and a window is a bound. They make an attack visible and expensive, not impossible.

The envelope signature check (§5.3) is a precondition, not one of the five. Every protection here assumes `from` has already been verified; run them on unverified envelopes and the (from, id) memory becomes forgeable.

Transport-level payload size (§18.9) is a separate bound with a separate owner. The sender-text cap does not replace it and cannot: it measures text after extraction, and it fires early on a sealed payload rather than late.

The fence does not touch the envelope. `payload.input` inside the verbatim signed envelope still holds the raw text, deliberately: rewriting it would break signature verification on a genuine message. Reaching past the fence to read it takes deliberate code, which is a documented escape hatch, not a hole.
